Hi,

Thank you for answering and spending time on my question.

https://www.dropbox.com/s/igv1rlcn3act2m8/sample1.bed?dl=0 —> This is the "bed" like methylation data from ENCODE RRBS. It is first 10k lines.
https://www.dropbox.com/s/240k2u1v5qzdch0/sample1.RData?dl=0 —> This is the granges object that I try to feed in methSeg() function and get the following error. I shared that newmeth object that I created with the following code.

myfile <- read.table('/Users/morova/Desktop/methylation/sample1.bed',sep = '\t',stringsAsFactors = F)
newmeth <- GRanges(seqnames = Rle(myfile[,"V1"]),ranges = IRanges(start = myfile[,"V2"],width = 1),
                   score = myfile[,"V11"]/100)
res=methSeg(newmeth,diagnostic.plot=TRUE,maxInt=100,minSeg=10)

This one is from tutorial which influenced me for trying methSegment.
In the context of methylation, we first extract segments between change points of the signal (methylation profiles) then cluster those segments into groups based on the mean methylation values of the segments. In this case, a segment is a region of the genome where CpGs have similar methylation values. We cluster those segments into segment groups using mixture modeling. The segment groups correspond to highly methylated regions or lowly methylated regions. Since this is an unsupervised method, we can find more patterns than just highly or lowly methylated regions. The users have to further overlap the segments with other marks and annotation such as promoters, H3K27ac or other histone modifications to associate segment groups with functional annotation.

T.

messages.body_plain:
My experimental design includes several variables:

Group (1 or 2)
Region (HIP or PFX)
Sex (M or F)

We have 5 replicates per unique combination of Group and Region:

HIP_GR1 (5 replicates)
PFX_GR1 (5 replicates)

HIP_GR2 (5 replicates)
PFX_GR2 (5 replicates)

There were 5 animals in Group1 and 5 animals in Group2; two brain regions were collected from each animal (HIP and PFX). So the 5 replicates of HIP_GR1 are the same animals as the 5 replicates of PFX_GR1, and the same goes for Group2.

We are primarily interested in the differences between the groups. I was planning to do contrasts as follows:

HIP_GR2 v HIP_GR1
PFX_GR2 v PFX_GR1

To include Sex, I was planning to add sex as a covariate.

I have a couple of questions:

1) Is there a difference between adding sex as a covariate or by splitting up my groups into males and females and making comparisons like this:

HIP_GR2_male v HIP_GR1_male
HIP_GR2_female v HIP_GR2_female

Also, when discussing with a colleague, they mentioned that we will need to take into account the correlation between brain regions that came from the same animal. I thought that the correlation between a pair of HIP and PFX Group 1 samples would not matter if we were simply comparing "like" brain regions to each other, but my colleague insists that

"when beta coefficients are estimated, covariance matrix will be used in the calculation. Therefore an inappropriate correlation structure will lead to biased estimation for beta coefficients. Let’s say the model is y=beta0+beta1*gender+beta2*group, to correctly estimate these betas, even though region is not even in the model, we still need to consider the correlation between regions."

2) What are your thoughts on including the correlation between samples that came from the same animal? For example, will I need to consider the correlation of HIP_GR1_replicate1 to PFX_GR1_replicate1 even if I am only comparing HIP_GR1 to HIP_GR2?

I hope this made sense, let me know if you need further clarification.

Thank you for your advice.

I have tried qvalue but compared to SLIM it leaves no significant hits behind (and this is a common feature regardless of the analysis package I've used so far).

I believe the lack of significance after p-value correction is due to the consistent right-hand skewed p-value distribution and therefore I have doubts whether or not I can actually trust the results I get. I also tried fdrtool in which you can use the test statistic values to acquire an empirical null distribution and then identify the q-value based on that; this leaves me with significant hits and p-value distribution that is uniform. If I run fdrtool with p-values instead it assumes normal null distribution (as does qvalue as I understood) and nothing remains significant. To my understanding the SLIM method is something of in between empirical and normal null expectation as it tries to fit several linears to the null distribution obtained from the data and by that obtain a correction factor used to get the q-values.

How big violations from normally distributed null model can SLIM handle in your opinion? All the examples of p-value distributions in Wang et al 2011 (the SLIM paper) are not as skewed as mine. I attached an example from methylKit but with I've seen even more even right-hand skewed distributions with other packages.

fit a logistic regression to methylation values where explanatory variable is the treatment (case or control). Compare the fit of the model with explanatory variable vs the null model (no explanatory variable) see if the fit is better using a Chisq test. the logistic regression response variables (methylation values) are weighted by their coverage.

in your case NAs have no effect, they are not in the model
